linkedin.text:
Before anyone lets an AI gateway hold their provider keys and see every agent call, someone has to sign off on it. Today we wrote the page for that person.

Control Tower's new security page answers the questions a reviewer actually asks:

What leaves our network? It runs on your servers, and there's no telemetry, crash reporting or analytics. The only outbound call is an optional daily Enterprise license renewal (the key and one number), and air-gapped installs turn it off.

How are secrets kept? Provider and tool credentials are encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a master key you hold, or stay in your own secret manager. Agents' keys are stored as SHA-256 hashes.

How do we know the image is yours? Every image and Helm chart is signed keylessly with Sigstore in CI, with an SBOM and build provenance. One cosign command checks it. Before release, CI also attacks each image with a forged license key, which it has to refuse.

It rounds out a busy week: six releases since Monday, including a Helm chart that runs one pod on SQLite or several on Postgres and Redis.

Read it, poke holes in it, open an issue if we got something wrong: https://github.com/joshmaster2165/controltower

A ⭐ helps other engineers find it.

#AIAgents #OpenSource #PlatformEngineering

posts:
Shipped today: a security page for whoever has to sign off on an AI gateway holding your provider keys.

No telemetry. Credentials AES-256-GCM under your key. Agent keys stored as hashes. Runs on your servers.

Don't take the page's word for it.

Every image is signed keylessly in CI with Sigstore, with an SBOM and build provenance. One `cosign verify` checks it.

And before release, CI attacks each image with a forged license key. It has to refuse.
Also this week: six releases since Monday, and a Helm chart. One pod on SQLite, or several on Postgres + Redis.

Self-hosted AI gateway for agents, models and MCP tools. A ⭐ helps other engineers find it:
https://github.com/joshmaster2165/controltower
